title: Sebastian and the Room
premise: Vesper Eriksen, a property surveyor sent to appraise the derelict Halvard house, discovers that its mirrors reflect a room one second behind reality — and that the room is singing. The song belongs to the dead who were walled inside it generations ago, and it wants a living voice to finish its last verse so it can finally stop. As Vesper is pulled deeper into the room's time-slip, they must choose between finishing the verse (which frees the dead but erases them) and refusing (which keeps them alive but leaves the room hungry for whoever comes next). In the end Vesper sings the verse wrong on purpose — a lullaby of mercy instead of a summons — collapsing the room and walking out with the mirrors finally showing only the present.
about_author: M. M. Vasquez is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties across the upper Midwest. Their fiction draws on the strange paperwork, sealed rooms, and unexplained silences of houses nobody wanted to buy.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Vesper arrives at the Halvard house to appraise it for demolition, POV theirs throughout. They note cold spots, a room missing from the blueprints, and a faint hum in the walls they file under 'settling structure.' Emotional beat: professional detachment as armor, already cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Still Vesper's POV. While photographing the hallway mirror, they notice their reflection lags — a blink arriving a beat too slow. Testing every mirror confirms it: all reflections show the same windowless room one second behind. Emotional beat: rational mind scrambling for explanations that keep dying.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Walls
chapters.summary: Vesper finds the previous surveyor's notes hidden in the fuse box, half a transcription of a song with its final verse torn away. That night, humming from inside the walls matches the notes exactly. Emotional beat: dread curdling into obsession; they can't leave the song unfinished.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Ada Halvard, 1911, through recovered diary pages interleaved with Vesper's research at the county archive. Ada describes her family sealing something — or someone — into the inner room during a fever winter. Emotional beat: guilt inherited like property, passed down unopened.

chapters.title: Pulled
chapters.summary: Vesper returns to photograph the mirrors and the lag widens to three seconds, then ten. When their reflection turns to look at them first, the room takes them — mid-step, mid-breath — into the windowless space where the song is loudest. Emotional beat: terror giving way to a horrible sense of arrival, of being expected.

chapters.title: The Occupants
chapters.summary: Inside the room, Vesper meets the faded dead: Ada among them, older now, still apologizing. They explain the bargain — a living voice must finish the verse to release them, but the singer becomes the room's new keeper. Emotional beat: pity tangled with self-preservation; Vesper starts falling for Ada's ghostly patience.

chapters.title: Duty Calls Collect
chapters.summary: Vesper's employer, unreachable for days, sends a replacement surveyor, Dana Okafor, whose POV alternates with Vesper's. Dana hears singing from the sealed room and reaches for the door. Vesper, watching through the mirror from inside, must decide whether to warn her off or let the room take someone else. Emotional beat: love against duty — Vesper chooses to protect a stranger at their own cost.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ada teaches Vesper the final verse, and Vesper realizes the song isn't a plea — it's an accusation, naming what the Halvards did. Singing it truly would free the dead but bind Vesper forever; refusing strands everyone. Emotional beat: the price of survival made explicit, itemized, non-negotiable.

chapters.title: Sung Wrong on Purpose
chapters.summary: Climax. With Dana breaking through the wall from outside and the room tightening around them, Vesper sings the last verse altered — turning the accusation into absolution, a lullaby instead of a summons. The dead let go, the mirrors shatter inward, and the room folds closed around Vesper as Dana pulls them through the breach. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, delivered as mercy.

chapters.title: Appraised at Nothing
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Vesper's POV. Weeks later, Vesper files the appraisal marking the house valueless and unsalvageable, then visits the empty lot after demolition. Every mirror they pass now shows only the present — but sometimes, in reflections, they hum four bars of a song they never learned. Emotional beat: survival with a scar; love outlasting the room that tried to keep it.
